h: Who made the pattern, and where to go next
p: The Great Garden at Pitmedden goes back to the late 1600s, when Sir Alexander Seton set out a formal garden on this site. Over the centuries the original planting was lost, and the patterns you see now were recreated in the twentieth century after the National Trust for Scotland took over, drawing on designs from the era. Knowing that it's a careful revival rather than a frozen relic makes it all the more impressive, because every one of those crisp lines takes serious effort to keep looking sharp.

Give it a couple of hours. Take a slow loop round the parterres, then head up for the higher view, and save some time for the farming collection and the woodland walk. Summer is when the bedding is at its most vivid, but the structure of the hedges looks smart even in the quieter months, and autumn brings apples to the orchard.

Just down the road is Tolquhon Castle, a romantic ruin looked after by Historic Environment Scotland, with an ornate gatehouse and plenty of carved details. It's an easy pairing, and it adds a bit of drama after the calm of the garden.

Haddo House and its country park are close by as well, so you could easily make a full day of it without much driving. Ellon itself has shops and cafés for lunch, and the coast at Newburgh, with its dunes and seal-watching, isn't far beyond. This part of Aberdeenshire is quiet, green and easy-going, which suits a garden day perfectly.
